newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil farmers seen ditching corn for soybeans.
newsitem.headline: Brazil farmers seen ditching corn for soybeans.

text.p: Brazilian farmers are likely to spurn corn in favor of soybeans when planting the 1997/98 crop after a dismal harvest of low market prices and weak industry demand, agronomists said.
"There is going to be a reduction of the order of 15.7 percent in planted area for corn," said Norberto Ortigara, director of Department of Rural Economy (Deral) in the key producing state of Parana.
"It's a buyers' market and industries have little desire to buy," he said.
Parana's planted area is set to drop to 1.3 million hectares in the 1997/98 harvest year, yielding between 5.2 and 5.7 million tonnes, down from 6.7 million tonnes in 1996/97.
"Farmers are opting for soybeans, which should see an increase of 260,000 hectares in planted area, and a small proportion are going for cotton," Ortigara said.

International prices have seen a sharp reversal since last year, encouraging industries to keep only a minimum of stocks, according to Vilmondes Olegario, director of agricultural supply at the Ministry of Agriculture.

"Last year, international prices rose sharply and everyone was building up large stocks, and they saw that this wasn't necessary anymore," said Olegario. "I think they are erring, only in the opposite direction."

Brazil was set to produce 34 million tonnes of corn in the main 1996/97 harvest and another 3.2 million tonnes during the second harvest, or safrinha, which spans July and August, independent consultant Safras e Mercado said.
But even though the safrinha will be 30 to 40 percent lower than originally expected because of drought in April and May, domestic prices have scarcely reacted.
Producers are receiving between 6.00 and 6.50 reais (US$5.55-6.00) per 60-kg bag, below the minimum price of 6.70 reais set by the government.

"Corn in Brazil is not an export product so it doesn't have the same liquidity as soybeans, as exporters are not competing for the product with domestic industries," said Safras analyst Paulo Molinari.
But he believes excessive government intervention is also to blame for lulling industries into relying on cheap sales of official stocks in the second half of the year.

"The government interfered too much in the market and has removed much of its liquidity," Molinari said. "Historically, Brazil buys expensive in the first half and sells cheaply in the second half of the year."

The government has already bought 2.6 million tonnes of corn out of planned purchases of 5.4 million tonnes, which will bring its total stocks up to 8.0 million tonnes by September/October, Olegario said.
"Our perception is that we are removing more than the surplus offer from the market. We are going to have to return at least 4.0 million tonnes to the market," Olegario said.
That same perception is keeping the market lacklustre, according to Molinari.

"The government has no interest in receiving all this corn," he said. "The industry saw this and reacted by taking a defensive position. Industries are going to pressure the government to start auctions from September."
Olegario says the government will not start auctions until the market hits a trigger price, to be decided next week, which is expected to be just under 8.50 reais per bag.
"Below that level, we have no interest in entering the market because we don't want to strangle private commercialisation," said Olegario.
The prospect of the market rising that far looks uncertain right now, with key indicators such as seed demand showing a marked lack of interest in the corn market.

"Seed producing firms are all extremely preoccupied," said Deral's Ortigara, noting that corn seed prices have fallen while soybean seed prices have soared. "They are desperate because they aren't managing to sell much corn."
